title: Europe: The Real Cost of Living

excluded.name: Russia
excluded.reason: Most of its territory and population statistics extend far beyond Europe, and comparable housing and income series are not published by Eurostat or the OECD after 2022.

excluded.name: Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan
excluded.reason: Often counted as transcontinental; they are not covered by the Eurostat house price, EU-SILC or HICP datasets used here.

excluded.name: Andorra, Liechtenstein, Monaco, San Marino, Vatican City
excluded.reason: Micro-states with almost no data in the comparable datasets used here. They are drawn on the map as context only.

prc_ppp_ind.name: Purchasing power parities and price level indices

indicators.label: House price growth
indicators.definition: Annual average change in the prices of all dwellings (new and existing) bought by households.
indicators.explainer: How much more (or less) homes cost on average this year compared with last year. 5% means a home that cost €100,000 last year now costs about €105,000.
indicators.caveat: For the United Kingdom, Greece, Switzerland, Serbia and North Macedonia growth is calculated from BIS central bank indices (annual averages of quarterly data). No comparable series exists for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo or Montenegro.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest quarter

indicators.label: House price index
indicators.definition: Index of the prices of all dwellings purchased by households, annual average, 2015 = 100.
indicators.explainer: An index tracks how prices change over time, not what a home actually costs. 150 means homes cost about 50% more than in 2015 in that country. It cannot tell you whether homes are cheaper in one country than another.
indicators.caveat: For the United Kingdom, Greece, Switzerland, Serbia and North Macedonia the series comes from the BIS, which republishes central bank data under national definitions (for example, Greece covers flats in urban areas). We converted it from quarterly to annual averages and rebased it to 2015 = 100. No official house price index is available in comparable form for Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Kosovo or Montenegro.

indicators.label: Real house prices
indicators.definition: Nominal house price index deflated by the private consumption deflator (OECD).
indicators.explainer: House prices with general inflation taken out. If this rises, homes are getting more expensive faster than everything else.

indicators.label: House price-to-income ratio
indicators.definition: Nominal house prices divided by nominal disposable income per head, expressed as an index (2015 = 100).
indicators.explainer: Compares house prices with what people earn. Above 100 means homes have become less affordable relative to incomes than they were in 2015; below 100 means more affordable. It shows change within a country, not which country is cheapest.
indicators.caveat: Published by the OECD for OECD members and a few partner countries only. No Western Balkan country is covered.

indicators.label: House price-to-rent ratio
indicators.definition: Nominal house price index divided by the rent component of the consumer price index (OECD), 2015 = 100.
indicators.explainer: Whether buying has become more expensive compared with renting. Rising values mean buying has pulled ahead of renting.

indicators.label: Rent inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the HICP sub-index for actual rentals paid by tenants (ECOICOP 04.1).
indicators.explainer: How fast rents for people who rent their home are rising. It follows existing and new rental contracts, so it moves more slowly than advertised rents.
indicators.caveat: Rents in many Balkan and Eastern European countries cover a small, often regulated, rental market. Rent weights in the price index are low where most people own their home.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Rent price index
indicators.definition: HICP annual average index for actual rentals for housing (ECOICOP 04.1), 2025 = 100 as published.
indicators.explainer: Tracks how rents change over time. 80 means rents were 20% lower than in 2025. Use "Indexed" view to pick a different base year.

indicators.label: Housing cost overburden rate
indicators.definition: Share of the population living in households where total housing costs (net of housing allowances) are more than 40% of disposable income (net of housing allowances).
indicators.explainer: The share of people who spend more than 40% of their household income on housing — rent or mortgage interest, utilities, repairs. A clear sign of housing stress.
indicators.caveat: Survey-based (EU-SILC). Western Balkan countries joined the survey later: North Macedonia from 2011, Serbia and Montenegro from 2013, Albania from 2017; Kosovo has a single year (2018). Bosnia and Herzegovina is not covered. Breaks in series are flagged.

indicators.label: Housing costs as a share of income
indicators.definition: Average share of total housing costs in disposable household income, all household types and income groups (EU-SILC).
indicators.explainer: The typical share of a household's income that goes on keeping a roof over its head, including rent or mortgage interest, utilities and maintenance.
indicators.caveat: This is the closest official measure to a rent-to-income ratio. We do not calculate our own rent-to-income ratio by combining unrelated datasets.

indicators.label: Consumer price inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (all items). Where no HICP exists, the national consumer price index reported by the World Bank is used and flagged.
indicators.explainer: How fast the prices of everyday goods and services are rising overall.
indicators.caveat: Bosnia and Herzegovina, the United Kingdom (no longer reported to Eurostat), Ukraine, Moldova and Belarus use national consumer price indices from the World Bank, which are not fully harmonised with the HICP.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Consumer price index
indicators.definition: HICP all-items annual average index (ECOICOP ver. 2), 2025 = 100 as published.
indicators.explainer: The general price level over time. 80 means everyday prices were 20% lower than in 2025.
indicators.caveat: Available only where a harmonised index exists; countries using a national CPI are not shown.

indicators.label: Food price inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the HICP for food and non-alcoholic beverages (ECOICOP 01).
indicators.explainer: How fast grocery prices are rising.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Household energy inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the HICP for electricity, gas and other fuels (ECOICOP 04.5).
indicators.explainer: How fast the cost of heating, cooling and powering a home is rising.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Transport price inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the HICP for transport (ECOICOP 07): vehicles, fuel, repairs and public transport.
indicators.explainer: How fast the cost of getting around is rising — from fuel to train tickets.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Housing & utilities inflation
indicators.definition: Annual average rate of change of the HICP for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels (ECOICOP 04).
indicators.explainer: Housing-related spending in the consumer basket: rents, water, repairs and energy. Owner-occupiers' mortgage costs and house purchases are not included.
indicators.latestLabel: Year-on-year change in the latest month

indicators.label: Price level of household consumption
indicators.definition: Price level index for actual individual consumption, based on purchasing power parities, EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive a country is compared with the EU average at a single point in time. 60 means the same basket of goods and services costs about 40% less than the EU average.

indicators.label: Price level of food
indicators.definition: Price level index for food (PPP-based), EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive food is compared with the EU average.

indicators.label: Price level of housing & utilities
indicators.definition: Price level index for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels (PPP-based), EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive rent (actual and imputed), water and energy are compared with the EU average.

indicators.label: Price level of household energy
indicators.definition: Price level index for electricity, gas and other fuels (PPP-based), EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive household energy is compared with the EU average.

indicators.label: Price level of transport
indicators.definition: Price level index for transport (PPP-based), EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive transport is compared with the EU average.

indicators.label: Price level of restaurants & hotels
indicators.definition: Price level index for restaurants and hotels (PPP-based), EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How expensive eating out and hotels are compared with the EU average.

indicators.label: Consumption per person (purchasing power)
indicators.definition: Actual individual consumption per capita in purchasing power standards, EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: How much people actually consume — goods and services, including those paid for by the state such as health and education — after adjusting for price differences. The best single measure of material well-being of households.

indicators.label: GDP per person (purchasing power)
indicators.definition: Gross domestic product per capita in purchasing power standards, EU-27 = 100.
indicators.explainer: Economic output per person, adjusted for price differences between countries.
indicators.caveat: GDP can overstate living standards in countries with many cross-border workers or large multinational profits (e.g. Luxembourg, Ireland).

indicators.label: Median household income (purchasing power)
indicators.definition: Median equivalised net income in purchasing power standards (EU-SILC).
indicators.explainer: What the household in the middle earns per adult-equivalent, after taxes and benefits, converted to a common currency that removes price differences between countries.
indicators.caveat: EU-SILC income refers to the year before the survey year.

indicators.label: Median household income (euro)
indicators.definition: Median equivalised net income in euro (EU-SILC).
indicators.explainer: The middle household's income in euro, without adjusting for price differences.
indicators.caveat: EU-SILC income refers to the year before the survey year.

indicators.label: Median household income (national currency)
indicators.definition: Median equivalised net income in national currency (EU-SILC).
indicators.explainer: Used only to compare how fast incomes grew within a country against house prices and rents. Values in different currencies cannot be compared across countries.
indicators.caveat: EU-SILC income refers to the year before the survey year.

indicators.label: GDP per person (international $)
indicators.definition: GDP per capita converted to international dollars using purchasing power parity rates (World Bank).
indicators.explainer: Output per person adjusted for prices, with the widest coverage — including Ukraine, Moldova and Belarus.
